offered_action_specs.name: rollback_deploy
offered_action_specs.description: Roll one service back to the settings it ran before its latest deploy, as the deploy log records them. Code plans it from that log, not from your tools' results, so you can name it even when they cannot see deploys: if the log holds no deploy of that service to undo, or the service changed since, code refuses it. Its container is recreated, so the service pauses while it restarts. Money already booked wrong stays wrong: a rollback stops new damage, and repairs nothing.

proposed.why: No tool calls are left. The evidence points to the payments-api database connection pool running out after the 21:42:25 deploy, probably leaked by the refund path.

findings.cause: payments-api's PostgreSQL connection pool (psycopg_pool) is empty, so requests wait for a connection, time out with PoolTimeout and return 500. Waiting for the pool is what drives p95 latency up. The 500s on POST /payments began at about 21:43:35, about 70 s after payments-api was redeployed at 21:42:25 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. The most likely mechanism is that each refund keeps its DB connection instead of returning it to the pool. Each refund that succeeded after the deploy would hold one connection until the pool ran out. Every route needing a connection then fails, POST /payments (the alert) and refunds alike. The provider is fast and Redis answers in under a millisecond, so neither causes the wait.

evidence.shows: The symptom is real. POST /payments 500s appear at 21:43:41 (1.1/s) and reach 5.8/s by 21:44:11, while 201s fall to 0.
The payments-api ERROR logs for POST /payments are all exception_type PoolTimeout, which means requests waited for a DB pool connection and gave up.

payments-api was redeployed at 21:42:25 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept (and PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents). It is the only change after the 21:40:58 stack start, about 1 minute before the errors.

Refunds succeeded (201) at about 0.13-0.44/s after the deploy, then stopped. From 21:43:35 both /payments and /refunds return 500, so the failure is shared across routes, as an empty pool would cause. The 503s (low, before the 500s) look like the provider breaker and are a separate, minor effect.
Refund requests from 21:43:28 on take about 5.0-6.9 s, consistent with a roughly 5 s pool wait timeout.
A 5 s refund trace has only Redis spans (sub-ms) and no provider or DB span. It ends in psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout, so it never got a connection. Redis is fast.

No refund that succeeded took over 500 ms. Connections are not held across slow calls, so the pool is not draining because of slow requests. This points to connections that are kept and never returned.
Provider call p95 stays at about 5-8 ms throughout, so fake-provider is not slow (this rules out the triage suspect). It does return some 500s, but quickly.

findings.left_open: No tool shows connections actually being kept or leaked by refunds. The link to REFUND_CONNECTION=kept rests on timing and on what the setting's name suggests. I did not check pool size, pool usage or PostgreSQL connections and locks, so it is still possible that something else holds connections, for example a DB-side lock or a different code path changed by the same deploy (PROVIDER_BREAKER, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT). I did not look into the provider's 500 answers or the 503s, and did not run the money check, so I don't know whether refunds or payments that failed after the provider call left our books out of step with the provider.

diagnosis.hypothesis: payments-api's psycopg connection pool is exhausted. Every request that needs a DB connection waits about 5 s, then fails with PoolTimeout and returns 500. This explains both the 5xx rate and the p95 of 7.4 s on POST /payments. The most likely cause is the 21:42:25 payments-api deploy with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept: each successful refund appears to keep its connection instead of returning it. From about 21:41:35 to 21:43:30, refunds succeeded at about 0.13-0.44/s with no slow ones. Then refunds and payments began failing together at 21:43:35. Steady, fast refunds followed by a shared failure across routes fits connections being kept, not held during slow calls. The provider and Redis are fast. This mechanism is inferred from timing and the setting's name; no result shows pool usage.

evidence.shows: POST /payments 500s appear at 21:43:41 (1.1/s) and rise to 5.82/s at 21:44:11, while 201s fall from about 3/s to 0.
Every payments-api ERROR line for POST /payments in the sample has exception_type PoolTimeout: requests gave up waiting for a DB pool connection.
payments-api was redeployed at 21:42:25 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents. Every other service dates from the 21:40:58 stack start.

Refund 201s run at 0.13-0.44/s from 21:41:35, then drop to 0 by 21:44:05. Both /payments and /refunds start returning 500 at 21:43:35. The failure is shared across routes, as an empty pool would cause. The small 503s on /payments predate the 500s and are a separate effect.
Refund requests from 21:43:28 on take about 5.0-6.9 s, consistent with a 5 s pool wait timeout plus queueing.

A 5,008 ms refund trace holds only two Redis spans (under 1 ms each) and no DB or provider span. It ends with error.type psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout, so it never got a connection and never reached the provider.
No successful refund took over 500 ms, so the pool is not draining because slow requests hold connections. This points to connections that are kept and never returned.
Provider call p95 stays at about 5-8 ms for both its 200s and its 500s, so fake-provider latency does not cause the waits.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it ran before the 21:42:25 deploy, which should remove REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. Recreating the container also drops every connection now held, so the pool starts empty. Afterwards, watch the POST /payments 5xx rate and p95 latency, and check that refund 201s keep going without the pool draining again. Then run the money check. Some payments or refunds may have failed after their provider call, and some 503s came from the breaker, so our books may be out of step with the provider's records. Still open: pool size and usage, and PostgreSQL connections and locks were never checked.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api pauses while its container is recreated, and payments and refunds in flight at that moment fail. The rollback reverts all three settings from that deploy, not only REFUND_CONNECTION. PROVIDER_BREAKER goes back to its earlier value. CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT, which affects charged amounts, also goes back to whatever it was before, and no result shows that value. If REFUND_CONNECTION is not the real cause, the pool may drain again later. Money already booked wrong stays wrong.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If the rollback makes things worse, redeploy payments-api with the 21:42:25 settings (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept), as recorded in the deploy log. Restart it whenever the pool drains, until a fix that keeps the other two settings is ready.
